title: Convolutional neural networks
html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

Before CNNs, image recognition systems were often split into two parts: a hand-designed feature extractor and a classifier. The feature extractor converted the raw image into features that the classifier could use. These systems often required the input to be carefully normalized, centered, or otherwise preprocessed to handle translations and distortions.

CNNs

There were three main additions that CNNs contributed; local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial or temporal subsampling.

local receptive fields

  • extract elementary visual features such as edges, endpoints, corners, etc...
  • combine these extracted elementary features with subsequent layers to extract higher order features

shared weights

  • force a set of units, whose receptive fields are located in different areas to share the same weights
  • elementary feature detectors that are useful in one part of an image are often useful in other areas too
  • these are called filters/kernels and perform the same operation on on different parts of the image which produce feature maps
  • a complete convolutional layer is composed of several differnt feature maps to extract various features

spatial or temporal subsampling

  • position of features is not really important and can in fact be harmful
  • 2x2 area that computes the average of the 4 inputs, multiplies it by a trainable coefficient, and adds a bias, passes the result to a sigmoid function
  • makes network less dependent on position variance

LeNet-5

The architecture consists of 7 layers. The input is a 32x32 image, values of input pixels are normalized so that the white corresponds to -0.1 and black corresponds to 1.175. LeNet showed that the same network could learn the feature extractor and classifier from raw pixels. Convolution allowed the network to learn features and exploit the spatial structure of images, shared weights, reduced the number of paramters, and subsampling made the representation less sensitive to small changes in feature positions.

layer C1

  • conv layer with 6 feaure maps
  • each feature map is connected to a 5x5 neighbohood in the input
  • (25+1)×6=156(25 + 1) \times 6 = 156(25+1)×6=156 learnable params

layer S2

  • subsampling layer with six feature maps of 14x14
  • each unit in the feature map is connected to a 2x2 neighborhood in the corresponding feature map in C1
  • the 2x2 receptive fields are nonoverlapping
  • 6×2=126 \times 2 = 126×2=12 learnable params

layer C3

  • conv layer with 16 feature maps
  • each one is connected to several 5x5 neighborhoods at identical locations of a subset of S2's feature maps
  • this forces a break of symmetry in the network
  • 6 C3 maps connect to 3 S2 maps
  • 9 C3 maps connect to 4 S2 maps
  • 1 C3 map connects to 6 S2 maps
  • (5×5×3+1)×6=456(5 \times 5 \times 3 + 1) \times 6 = 456(5×5×3+1)×6=456
  • (5×5×4+1)×9=909(5 \times 5 \times 4 + 1) \times 9 = 909(5×5×4+1)×9=909
  • (5×5×6+1)=151(5 \times 5 \times 6 + 1) = 151(5×5×6+1)=151
  • 456+909+151=1516456 + 909 + 151 = 1516456+909+151=1516 learnable params

layer S4

  • subsampling layer with 16 feature maps of size 5x5
  • each feature map is connected to a 2x2 neighborhood in the corresponding feature map in C3
  • 16×2=3216 \times 2 = 3216×2=32 learnable params

layer C5

  • conv layer with 120 feature maps
  • each unit is connected to a 5x5 neighborhood on all 16 of S4's feature maps
  • (5×5×16+1)×120=48120(5 \times 5 \times 16 + 1) \times 120 = 48120(5×5×16+1)×120=48120 learnable params

layer F6

  • 84 units and is fully connected to C5
  • 121×84=10164121 \times 84 = 10164121×84=10164 learnable params

ouput layer

  • the ouput layer is Euclidiean RBF units, one for each class with 84 inputs each
  • the ouputs of each unit is computed as follows yh=∑j(xj−wij)2 y_h = \sum_j (x_j - w_{ij})^2 yh​=j∑​(xj​−wij​)2
  • bassically measuring the distance between the 84 input vector and the known vector for the class

loss

  • use a more discriminative loss that makes the correct class's distance small while making the incorrect classes' distances large
  • use backprop to train all the CNN weights, since conv layers share weights, their gradients must be summed across all the connections that use the shared weights

AlexNet

Eight learned layers; 5 convolutional, 3 fully connected. It showed that large/deep CNNs coudl acheive major gains on ImageNet. Demonstrated that CNNs could scale to millions of high-resolution images. GPU training made much larger CNNs practical

ReLU

  • LeNet-5 used sigmoid or tanh activation functions. When the input is very positive, sigmoid gets close to 1. When the input is very negative, sigmoid gets close to 0. In both regions, the curve becomes almost flat. this is a problem because the this means the gradient becomes tiny. so if each layer has a small gradient and you are mulitplying repeatedly by small numbers, you have a vanishing gradient problem
  • relu is max(0,x)max(0, x)max(0,x), so for positive values f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x, therefore f′(x)=1f'(x) = 1f′(x)=1
  • so the gradient can pass through without being shrunk by the activation function
  • AlexNet was a huge CNN and around 60 million parameters.
  • one problem with ReLU is that for negative inputs the gradient is 0. so a neuron that stays negative can stop recieving gradietn through ReLU. this is related to the dying ReLU problem
  • currently: smoother ReLU alternatives (GELU/SiLU)

local response normalization

  • makes nearby CNN filters compete with each other
  • LRN looks at nearby activations and divides each activation by a value based on how big the neighboring activations are
  • this encourages network to a distinctive feature responses instead of letting many filter become active at the same time bi=ai(k+α∑jaj2)β b_i = \frac{a_i}{\left(k + \alpha \sum_j a_j^2\right)^\beta} bi​=(k+α∑j​aj2​)βai​​ overlapping pooling
  • Overlapping pooling means the pooling windows share some of the input. AlexNet found this generalized slightly better than non-overlapping pooling.

ResNet

  • training framework to ease the training of deeper networks
  • deeper networks can actually perform worse because it is harder to optimize, this is called the degredation problem
  • isntead of letting layers fit a desired mapping, they let them fit a residual
  • h(x)=f(x)+xh(x) = f(x) + xh(x)=f(x)+x

title: Attention
html:
Attention allows the model to focus on the relevant parts of the input sequence. Self attention connects everything directly. In the sentence "The cat sat on the mat", "sat" can directly attend to "mat"

RNN + LSTM processes the sentence sequentially, so if "sat" and "mat" were 50 words apart, it would have to travel through 50 hiddent states. This matters because gradients have to also travel along this path during training making it harder to make the connection between the words. You also are not able to fully parallelize RNNs since they use recursion, whereas using attention you can calcuate Q, K, V for all token simultaneously.

CNN models can only see a small local region at a time, so they need multiple layers to connect far apart tokens

title: Transformers
html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

The transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on Attention to compute representations of its input and output without sequence aligned RNN + LSTM or CNN.

Encoder

  • stack of 6 identical layers, each layer has two sub-layers
  • multi-head self-attention and a simply position wise fully connected feed-forward neural network
  • residual connection around each of the sublayers + layer normalization

Decoder

  • stack of 6 identical layers
  • third sublayer, performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack

Position-Wise FFN

  • two linear transformations with a ReLU activation between them

Positional encoding

One catch: attention is permutation-invariant. Without positional information, the model can't tell the difference between "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". The original paper handles this with sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the input embeddings.

Sinusoidal positional encoding is rarely used now. Modern models lean on rotary position encoding (RoPE) or attention with linear biases (ALiBi) instead.

The original transformer was also designed for translation, an encoder-decoder setup. Today, the dominant variant is decoder-only (GPT-style), which keeps just the masked self-attention side of the original architecture.

KV caching

When a decoder-only model generates text, it produces one token at a time. Naively, each new token would recompute attention over the entire sequence from scratch, including all the keys and values for tokens that haven't changed since the last step. That's wasteful.

The trick: for each token we generate, we cache its K and V vectors. On the next step, we only compute K and V for the new token and append them to the cache. We still compute a fresh Q for the new token (since it's the one doing the looking), but the keys and values it attends to are read from the cache.

This turns generation from quadratic to linear per step. The tradeoff is memory, the KV cache grows with sequence length and quickly dominates GPU memory for long contexts.

Grouped-query attention (GQA)

Standard multi-head attention gives every head its own Q, K, and V projections. If you have 32 heads, you're storing 32 separate K and V tensors per layer in the KV cache. Painful.

Multi-query attention (MQA) went to the other extreme: all heads share a single K and V, with only Q being per-head. Way smaller cache, but quality drops.

Grouped-query attention is the compromise that won: heads are split into groups, and each group shares one K and V. So 32 query heads might map to 8 KV heads. You get most of the quality of full multi-head attention with a fraction of the cache size. Llama 2/3, Mistral, and most current open models use GQA.

- two linear transformations with a relu activation between them

 positional encoding

one catch: attention is permutation-invariant. without positional information, the model can't tell the difference between "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". the original paper handles this with sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the input embeddings.

sinusoidal positional encoding is rarely used now. modern models lean on rotary position encoding (rope) or attention with linear biases (alibi) instead.

the original transformer was also designed for translation, an encoder-decoder setup. today, the dominant variant is decoder-only (gpt-style), which keeps just the masked self-attention side of the original architecture.

 kv caching

when a decoder-only model generates text, it produces one token at a time. naively, each new token would recompute attention over the entire sequence from scratch, including all the keys and values for tokens that haven't changed since the last step. that's wasteful.

the trick: for each token we generate, we cache its k and v vectors. on the next step, we only compute k and v for the new token and append them to the cache. we still compute a fresh q for the new token (since it's the one doing the looking), but the keys and values it attends to are read from the cache.

this turns generation from quadratic to linear per step. the tradeoff is memory, the kv cache grows with sequence length and quickly dominates gpu memory for long contexts.

 grouped-query attention (gqa)

standard multi-head attention gives every head its own q, k, and v projections. if you have 32 heads, you're storing 32 separate k and v tensors per layer in the kv cache. painful.

multi-query attention (mqa) went to the other extreme: all heads share a single k and v, with only q being per-head. way smaller cache, but quality drops.

grouped-query attention is the compromise that won: heads are split into groups, and each group shares one k and v. so 32 query heads might map to 8 kv heads. you get most of the quality of full multi-head attention with a fraction of the cache size. llama 2/3, mistral, and most current open models use gqa.

title: DINO
html:
DINO (self-distillation with no labels) is a self-supervised method for learning visual representations from unlabeled images. The paper's central finding is that self-supervised Vision Transformers develop semantic structure that is less apparent in supervised ViTs and CNNs: their features work well for k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) classification, and some attention maps reveal foreground objects and boundaries.

Why self-supervision?

A supervised image classifier may receive one class label for an image that also contains objects, textures, boundaries, and spatial relationships. DINO instead creates a learning signal from different augmented views of the same image. It asks the model to produce consistent outputs across changes in crop, scale, and appearance, without human class labels or segmentation masks.

Student and teacher

DINO uses two networks with the same architecture: a student gθsg_{\theta_s}gθs​​ and a teacher gθtg_{\theta_t}gθt​​. Given an unlabeled image xxx, it creates different views x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​:

x⟶(x1,x2),x1→studentps(x1),x2→teacherpt(x2). x \longrightarrow (x_1,x_2), \qquad x_1 \xrightarrow{\text{student}} p_s(x_1), \qquad x_2 \xrightarrow{\text{teacher}} p_t(x_2). x⟶(x1​,x2​),x1​student​ps​(x1​),x2​teacher​pt​(x2​).

The student learns to match the teacher's output distribution for another view of the same image. In simplified form, the cross-entropy objective is

L=−∑kpt(k)(x2)log⁡ps(k)(x1). \mathcal{L}=-\sum_k p_t^{(k)}(x_2)\log p_s^{(k)}(x_1). L=−k∑​pt(k)​(x2​)logps(k)​(x1​).

These output dimensions are not predefined class labels such as dog or car. The useful image representation is learned through this training task.

Teacher update: exponential moving average

Only the student receives gradients. The teacher output is treated as a fixed target during a student update; afterward, the teacher parameters follow the student by an exponential moving average (EMA):

θt←mθt+(1−m)θs. \theta_t \leftarrow m\theta_t+(1-m)\theta_s. θt​←mθt​+(1−m)θs​.

With mmm close to 111, the teacher changes more slowly than the student. It acts as a smoothed history of student parameters and provides a relatively stable target. EMA makes the target stable, not automatically meaningful. Both networks start without semantic knowledge; useful structure emerges gradually across images and augmentations.

Why doesn't it collapse?

Matching two views admits a trivial solution: map every image to the same output. DINO uses centering and sharpening of the teacher output to discourage this representation collapse.

Centering

DINO tracks a running center ccc of the teacher's output logits and subtracts it before the teacher softmax. If one output dimension dominates across many images, its average grows and centering suppresses it:

zt⟶zt−c. z_t \longrightarrow z_t-c. zt​⟶zt​−c.

This discourages all images from activating the same dominant output dimensions.

Sharpening

The teacher uses a low-temperature softmax:

pt(k)(x)=exp⁡ ⁣((zt(k)(x)−ck)/τt)∑jexp⁡ ⁣((zt(j)(x)−cj)/τt). p_t^{(k)}(x)= \frac{\exp\!\left((z_t^{(k)}(x)-c_k)/\tau_t\right)} {\sum_j\exp\!\left((z_t^{(j)}(x)-c_j)/\tau_t\right)}. pt(k)​(x)=∑j​exp((zt(j)​(x)−cj​)/τt​)exp((zt(k)​(x)−ck​)/τt​)​.

A smaller teacher temperature τt\tau_tτt​ makes its output distribution more peaked and discourages uninformative, nearly uniform targets. In short, centering counters a globally dominant output, while sharpening counters a uniform output.

Multi-crop training

DINO creates views at multiple scales. The teacher receives global crops; the student receives global and local crops. For example, a student view containing a dog's head may be trained to match the teacher's output for a larger view containing much of the dog.

This encourages local visual information to remain consistent with a broader view of the same image. It is an intuitive explanation for the learned structure, not a claim that DINO is explicitly taught object parts or identities. The paper also finds that smaller ViT patches improve the learned visual features.

What emerges?

  • Semantically useful embeddings: Related images tend to be near one another in the learned feature space. A new image can be classified by finding nearby labeled training images and using their labels. With a small ViT, DINO reached 78.3% ImageNet top-1 accuracy using k-NN, without training a classifier on top of its features.
  • Object-like attention: Some attention heads in the final ViT block highlight foreground objects and approximate their boundaries. These are segmentation-like patterns in attention maps; DINO was not trained with segmentation masks.

The paper reports that these properties are less apparent in supervised ViTs and convolutional networks.

title: DINOv2
html:
DINOv2 is a family of pretrained Vision Transformers that turns an image into general-purpose visual features. It learns from images without class labels or captions. The goal is a visual backbone whose features transfer across image distributions and tasks, often with the backbone frozen and a small task-specific head trained on top.

DINOv2 combines DINO-style image-level self-distillation, iBOT-style masked patch learning, carefully curated data, and large-scale training.

What the encoder produces

A ViT divides an image into patches and returns both an image-level representation and spatial patch tokens:

image→DINOv2(zimage, z1,z2,…,zN). \text{image}\xrightarrow{\text{DINOv2}} \left(z_{\mathrm{image}},\,z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_N\right). imageDINOv2​(zimage​,z1​,z2​,…,zN​).

Feature What it captures Example uses
Image-level feature Overall image content Classification, retrieval, object recognition
Patch features Information tied to image regions Segmentation, depth estimation, other dense tasks

The patch features are useful because a task can retain where information appears, rather than relying only on one vector for the entire image.

How DINOv2 learns

1. Match different views of an image

As in DINO, a student and a slowly updated teacher process different augmented views of the same image. The student learns to match the teacher's image-level output:

x→(x1,x2)→consistent image-level outputs. x\rightarrow(x_1,x_2) \rightarrow \text{consistent image-level outputs}. x→(x1​,x2​)→consistent image-level outputs.

This encourages features that remain useful across changes such as crop, scale, and color. The teacher's exponential moving average (EMA) update supplies a stable target during self-supervised training.

2. Predict masked patch outputs

DINOv2 also uses an iBOT-style patch objective. Some patches are masked in the student view; the teacher sees the corresponding unmasked image. At the masked positions, the student predicts the teacher's patch-level outputs.

masked student patches⟶teacher outputs for those patches. \text{masked student patches} \longrightarrow \text{teacher outputs for those patches}. masked student patches⟶teacher outputs for those patches.

Together, the two objectives train global image features and local spatial features. The model is predicting learned teacher outputs, not reconstructing raw pixels or using segmentation labels.

What makes DINOv2 stronger?

Ingredient Role
Curated data An automated pipeline filters and balances diverse images. The resulting LVD-142M dataset contains about 142 million images.
Larger ViTs The largest model, ViT-g/14, has about 1.1 billion parameters; “/14” denotes 14×1414\times1414×14 pixel patches.
Training at scale The paper combines and adapts self-supervised methods to make large-model training more stable and efficient.
Distillation A large trained model transfers its representations to smaller ViTs that are cheaper to run.

Two kinds of teacher: The EMA teacher provides targets while the large model is learning from images. During model distillation, the already trained large model teaches smaller models. These are different stages with different purposes.

Data curation matters as much as scale: the paper reports stronger transfer on most tested benchmarks from curated LVD-142M than from uncurated images.

Why the features matter

DINOv2 is evaluated on both image-level tasks, such as classification and retrieval, and pixel-level tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation. These tasks can use a frozen visual backbone with a trained probe or decoder; “no fine-tuning” refers to the backbone, not to every downstream component.

Possible use in robotics

A robotics system needs more than an image-level label like “cup.” It may need features for object regions, boundaries, parts, and scene layout. DINOv2 patch tokens can serve as pretrained visual inputs to a policy or world model:

RGB image→DINOv2 patch tokens→policy or world model. \text{RGB image} \rightarrow \text{DINOv2 patch tokens} \rightarrow \text{policy or world model}. RGB image→DINOv2 patch tokens→policy or world model.

This is a possible application of the learned spatial features, not a robotics benchmark reported by the paper.

DINOv2 compared with DINO and CLIP

DINO DINOv2 CLIP
Training input Images Images Image–text pairs
Main learning signal Match views of the same image Match views and masked patch outputs Match images with captions
Emphasis Self-supervised semantic structure Transferable global and spatial features at scale Language-aligned visual features

DINOv2 builds on DINO's teacher–student approach and adds patch-level learning, curated data at scale, larger models, and distillation into smaller ones. CLIP uses text supervision, making its features directly aligned with language. Both CLIP and DINOv2 learn semantic information, but their training signals emphasize different properties.

142M curated images → image-level + patch-level self-supervision → large ViT → smaller distilled models → reusable visual features.

title: CLIP
html:
Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) learns image representations by matching images to their captions. It was trained from scratch on roughly 400 million image–text pairs collected from the internet. In the original paper, its zero-shot ImageNet accuracy matched that of a supervised ResNet-50 without training on ImageNet's 1.28 million labeled training images.

Core idea

A conventional image classifier maps an image to one of a fixed set of labels. CLIP instead learns a shared embedding space in which an image and text describing it are close together:

I→fθzI,T→gϕzT,zI,zT∈Rd. I \xrightarrow{f_\theta} z_I, \qquad T \xrightarrow{g_\phi} z_T, \qquad z_I,z_T\in\mathbb{R}^d. Ifθ​​zI​,Tgϕ​​zT​,zI​,zT​∈Rd.

For example, a dog image should be more similar to “a photo of a dog” than to “a photo of an airplane.” This connection between visual and language concepts is called vision–language alignment.

Architecture

CLIP has two independently run encoders:

  • Image encoder: A ResNet or Vision Transformer converts an image into a feature vector, which is projected into the shared embedding space. With a ViT, the path is image → patches → Transformer → projection → image embedding.
  • Text encoder: A Transformer converts caption tokens into a feature vector, which is projected into the same space.

The projected vectors are normalized before comparison. CLIP has no cross-attention between image and text: the encoders process their inputs separately, and their outputs meet through similarity scores.

Contrastive training

For a batch of NNN matched pairs (Ii,Ti)(I_i,T_i)(Ii​,Ti​), CLIP computes the similarity of every image with every caption. The diagonal entries are matching, or positive, pairs; the other entries are in-batch negative pairs.

T1T_1T1​ T2T_2T2​ T3T_3T3​
I1I_1I1​ ✓ × ×
I2I_2I2​ × ✓ ×

Similarity is based on the cosine of the angle between normalized embeddings:

sim⁡(zI,zT)=zI⊤zT∥zI∥∥zT∥. \operatorname{sim}(z_I,z_T)=\frac{z_I^\top z_T}{\lVert z_I\rVert\lVert z_T\rVert}. sim(zI​,zT​)=∥zI​∥∥zT​∥zI⊤​zT​​.

Aligned vectors have similarity near 111; orthogonal vectors have similarity near 000. CLIP scales the similarity scores with a learned temperature, then applies a softmax to each row and column. Cross-entropy loss trains it in both directions:

  1. Given an image, identify its matching caption.
  2. Given a caption, identify its matching image.

Together, these objectives increase the scores of matching pairs relative to the other pairs in the batch.

Zero-shot classification

After training, CLIP can classify an image using text descriptions of candidate classes, without fitting a new classifier for those classes:

  1. Turn each class into a prompt, such as “a photo of a dog,” “a photo of a cat,” and “a photo of a car.”
  2. Encode the image and all three prompts.
  3. Predict the class whose prompt has the highest image–text similarity.

For a golden retriever image, the dog prompt should score highest. The candidate prompts define the classes at inference time, so the result depends in part on the wording of those prompts.

Limitations

  • Limited joint reasoning: The separate encoders learn broad semantic alignment, but do not jointly inspect image and text in the way models with cross-modal interaction can.
  • Training-data dependence: Missing concepts and biases in web image–text pairs can carry into CLIP's representations and predictions.
  • Loss of fine detail: Distinguishing matching captions does not require retaining every visual detail. Precise geometry and spatial relationships may matter more in tasks such as robotics.

title: Mixture of Experts
html:
In a dense model, every example activates the same set of parameters. As both model size and the number of training examples grow, training becomes more expensive. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer increases model capacity without activating every parameter for every input: a trainable gating network (or router) selects only a few experts to process each input.

In the Sparsely-Gated MoE paper, the experts are feed-forward networks (MLPs) with the same architecture but separate learned weights. The gate and experts are trained jointly by backpropagation.

How an MoE layer works

Let E1,E2,…,EnE_1, E_2, \ldots, E_nE1​,E2​,…,En​ be the experts. For an input xxx, the gate produces a sparse vector G(x)G(x)G(x), where G(x)iG(x)_iG(x)i​ is the weight assigned to expert iii. The layer output is

y=∑i=1nG(x)iEi(x). y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} G(x)_i E_i(x). y=i=1∑n​G(x)i​Ei​(x).

For example, if five experts have gate weights

G(x)=[0, 0.7, 0, 0.3, 0], G(x) = [0,\ 0.7,\ 0,\ 0.3,\ 0], G(x)=[0, 0.7, 0, 0.3, 0],

then only experts 2 and 4 run, and their outputs are combined as

y=0.7E2(x)+0.3E4(x). y = 0.7E_2(x) + 0.3E_4(x). y=0.7E2​(x)+0.3E4​(x).

Experts with zero gate weight do not need to be evaluated for that input.

Gating and routing

Softmax gating multiplies the input by a trainable weight matrix and applies softmax:

Gsoftmax(x)=softmax⁡(xWg). G_{\text{softmax}}(x) = \operatorname{softmax}(xW_g). Gsoftmax​(x)=softmax(xWg​).

This gives every expert a nonzero weight, so it does not provide sparse computation.

Noisy top-kkk gating adds Gaussian noise with a learned scale to the scores, keeps the kkk highest scores, sets all others to −∞-\infty−∞, and then applies softmax. The excluded experts therefore receive weight zero. The noise helps prevent the gate from settling on a small group of experts too early.

Balancing expert use

Without balancing, the gate may send most inputs to a few experts. Those experts then receive more training, which can make the imbalance worse. For a batch BBB, the paper defines each expert's importance as its total gate weight:

Importance⁡(Ei)=∑x∈BG(x)i. \operatorname{Importance}(E_i) = \sum_{x \in B} G(x)_i. Importance(Ei​)=x∈B∑​G(x)i​.

An auxiliary importance loss encourages these totals to be similar across experts. The paper also uses a separate load loss to balance how many inputs are routed to each expert: equal total gate weights alone do not guarantee equal numbers of inputs.

The shrinking batch problem

If a batch contains bbb inputs and each input selects kkk of nnn experts, then each expert receives about kb/nkb/nkb/n inputs when routing is balanced. As nnn grows, these small expert batches make GPU computation less efficient.

The paper addresses this by increasing the effective batch size. Ordinary layers and gates use data parallelism, while experts are distributed across devices. At the MoE layer, inputs from all devices are grouped by their selected expert, so each expert processes a larger combined batch.

title: Mixture of Transformers
html:
Mixture of Transformers (MoT) is a multimodal architecture that gives text, image, and speech tokens separate Transformer parameters while keeping global self-attention across the full sequence. A token uses the parameters for its own modality, but it can still attend to tokens from every modality. This increases total model capacity without increasing the amount of Transformer computation used by each token at a fixed model width.

Why separate parameters by modality?

An early-fusion multimodal Transformer puts text, image, and speech tokens in one sequence and processes them with shared parameters. These modalities have different structures: text is discrete and linguistic, images are spatial, and speech has temporal and acoustic structure.

The paper gives several reasons to consider separate parameters:

  • Training is expensive. Chameleon used 9.2 trillion multimodal tokens to reach text performance comparable to LLaMA 2 trained on 2 trillion text tokens. These token counts include different data mixes, so they are an illustration rather than a controlled comparison.
  • Training objectives can interfere. Updates that help one modality may not help another, especially when modalities use different objectives.
  • Representations separate anyway. In a dense multimodal model, the authors used principal component analysis (PCA) to visualize hidden states and found that text, image, and speech tokens occupied distinct regions of the feature space.

A Mixture of Experts also provides sparse computation, but its learned router can use experts unevenly and make training harder to balance. MoT uses each token's known modality to choose its parameters.

How MoT works

For each modality, MoT has separate attention projection matrices, feed-forward networks (FFNs), and layer normalization parameters. If token xix_ixi​ has modality mim_imi​, its query, key, and value are projected with that modality's weights:

Qi=xiWQmi,Ki=xiWKmi,Vi=xiWVmi. Q_i = x_i W_Q^{m_i}, \qquad K_i = x_i W_K^{m_i}, \qquad V_i = x_i W_V^{m_i}. Qi​=xi​WQmi​​,Ki​=xi​WKmi​​,Vi​=xi​WVmi​​.

For example, a text token uses WQtextW_Q^{\text{text}}WQtext​, while an image token uses WQimageW_Q^{\text{image}}WQimage​. The same modality-specific choice applies to the key, value, output projection, FFN, and layer norms.

Attention remains global: after the modality-specific projections, queries, keys, and values are restored to their original sequence order. Each token can attend to text, image, and speech tokens in the same attention operation. The attention output then passes through the output projection and FFN for that token's modality.

At a fixed model width, each token runs one set of projections and one FFN, as it would in a dense Transformer. The model stores more parameters because it has a separate set for each modality, but only the relevant set is active for a given token.

Reported results

In the paper's Chameleon text-and-image setting, a 7B MoT model matched the dense baseline's performance using 55.8% of its training FLOPs. With speech added as a third modality, it reached comparable speech performance with 37.2% of the dense baseline's FLOPs for speech. These comparisons refer to the training needed to reach similar performance; a MoT layer at the same width has the same per-token FLOP count as a dense layer.

Source

Liang et al., Mixture-of-Transformers: A Sparse and Scalable Architecture for Multi-Modal Foundation Models

html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

autoencoder.py trains a VAE on MNIST. The checked-in latent space and interpolation images show example outputs. The note below explains the probabilistic objective behind the code.

See also the shorter Autoencoder note for the deterministic starting point.

A VAE learns to generate data from latent variables. Its encoder maps an example to a distribution over latent vectors, and its decoder maps a sampled latent vector to a distribution over possible outputs.

1. Intuition: why latent variables?

Imagine generating handwritten digits. Sampling each pixel independently would ignore the structure of the image: the top and bottom halves need to form a coherent digit.

Instead, we introduce a latent vector zzz: a hidden representation that can capture factors such as digit shape, stroke thickness, and slant. These factors are learned from data; we do not explicitly assign a meaning to each coordinate.

The decoder uses this shared latent vector to generate a coherent image. Even if it models pixels as independent given zzz, they can still be dependent overall because they share the same zzz.

Notation

Symbol Meaning
xxx An observed example, such as an image
zzz A latent vector
p(z)p(z)p(z) Prior: a distribution over latent vectors before observing xxx
pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x\mid z)pθ​(x∣z) Decoder: a distribution over outputs given zzz
pθ(z∣x)p_\theta(z\mid x)pθ​(z∣x) True posterior: a distribution over latent vectors given xxx
qϕ(z∣x)q_\phi(z\mid x)qϕ​(z∣x) Encoder: a learned approximation to the true posterior
θ,ϕ\theta,\phiθ,ϕ Decoder and encoder parameters, respectively

2. The generative process

To generate a new image:

  1. Sample a latent vector from a simple prior, usually z∼N(0,I)z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)z∼N(0,I).
  2. Use the decoder to sample an image: x∼pθ(x∣z)x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z)x∼pθ​(x∣z).

The neural network learns how to turn simple Gaussian latent vectors into a complex distribution over images.

What do we want to maximize?

We want the model to assign high likelihood to the training data. The likelihood of one image sums over all possible latent explanations:

pθ(x)=∫pθ(x∣z) p(z) dz p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz pθ​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z)p(z)dz

Training aims to maximize the sum of log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) across the dataset.

The difficulty: For a neural decoder, this integral is generally intractable to evaluate exactly. Estimating it by sampling from the prior can also be inefficient: most sampled latent vectors may assign very low likelihood to a particular training image.

3. The true posterior: which latent vectors explain an image?

Generation goes from zzz to xxx. Given an observed image, we also want to reason in the other direction: which latent vectors could have produced it?

Bayes' rule gives the answer:

pθ(z∣x)=pθ(x∣z) p(z)pθ(x) p_\theta(z\mid x) =\frac{p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{p_\theta(x)} pθ​(z∣x)=pθ​(x)pθ​(x∣z)p(z)​

This is the true posterior for the current generative model.

The difficulty: Its denominator is the same intractable likelihood from the previous section, so we cannot usually evaluate the posterior directly.

4. The encoder: approximate the true posterior

We introduce an encoder that learns an approximation:

qϕ(z∣x)≈pθ(z∣x) q_\phi(z\mid x)\approx p_\theta(z\mid x) qϕ​(z∣x)≈pθ​(z∣x)

Given an image of a 777, the encoder should concentrate probability on latent vectors that help the decoder reconstruct that particular 777.

The encoder outputs a distribution, rather than just a single vector. A common choice is a Gaussian whose mean and variance are predicted by a neural network:

qϕ(z∣x)=N ⁣(z;μϕ(x),diag⁡(σϕ2(x))) q_\phi(z\mid x) =\mathcal N\!\left(z;\mu_\phi(x),\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x))\right) qϕ​(z∣x)=N(z;μϕ​(x),diag(σϕ2​(x)))

During training, we sample from this distribution to obtain latent vectors suited to the input. To generate new images after training, we sample from the prior p(z)p(z)p(z) and use the decoder.

5. KL divergence: measure the approximation gap

KL divergence measures a discrepancy between two probability distributions. Here, we use it to compare the encoder with the true posterior:

DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x))=Ez∼qϕ(z∣x)[log⁡qϕ(z∣x)−log⁡pθ(z∣x)] D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z\mid x)\right) =\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi(z\mid x)} \left[ \log q_\phi(z\mid x)-\log p_\theta(z\mid x) \right] DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x))=Ez∼qϕ​(z∣x)​[logqϕ​(z∣x)−logpθ​(z∣x)]

Read this as three steps:

  1. Sample zzz from the encoder distribution.
  2. Compare the log densities assigned to zzz by the encoder and the true posterior.
  3. Average the difference over the encoder distribution.

KL divergence is nonnegative and equals zero when the distributions match almost everywhere. It is not symmetric, so the order of the distributions matters.

We cannot evaluate this KL directly because it contains the true posterior. Instead, we use Bayes' rule to rearrange it into a tractable training objective.

6. The ELBO: an objective we can optimize

Substituting Bayes' rule into the KL expression gives:

DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x))=log⁡pθ(x)−Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]+DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z)). \begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z\mid x)\right) &=\log p_\theta(x) -\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]\\ &\quad+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\right). \end{aligned} DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x))​=logpθ​(x)−Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]+DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z)).​

Rearranging yields:

log⁡pθ(x)=LELBO(x)+DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ pθ(z∣x)) \log p_\theta(x) =\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x) +D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z\mid x)\right) logpθ​(x)=LELBO​(x)+DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥pθ​(z∣x))

where the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is:

LELBO(x)=Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]⏟reconstruction term−DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z))⏟prior regularization \boxed{ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x) =\underbrace{\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]}_{\text{reconstruction term}} -\underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\right)}_{\text{prior regularization}} } LELBO​(x)=reconstruction termEqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]​​−prior regularizationDKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z))​​​

Because the posterior KL is nonnegative, LELBO(x)≤log⁡pθ(x)\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\leq\log p_\theta(x)LELBO​(x)≤logpθ​(x). We train both networks by maximizing this lower bound, usually estimating the reconstruction expectation with samples.

Term What optimizing it encourages
Reconstruction term Latent vectors that let the decoder assign high likelihood to the input
Prior regularization Encoder distributions that stay close to the prior used for generation

Keep the two KL terms distinct: The KL to the true posterior is the gap between the ELBO and the log likelihood. The KL to the prior is the regularizer we actually evaluate in the objective.

When implementing training as a minimization problem, use the negative ELBO:

VAE loss=−Eqϕ(z∣x)[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]+DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣x) ∥ p(z)) \text{VAE loss} =-\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)] +D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\right) VAE loss=−Eqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]+DKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∥p(z))

uv run python 02-generative-models/02-ddpm/train.py --download --epochs 1

A DDPM learns to generate images by reversing a gradual noising process. During training, it predicts the noise in a corrupted real image. During generation, it starts from Gaussian noise and repeatedly takes a small step toward a cleaner image.

1. The two processes

Forward diffusion is a fixed procedure that progressively destroys image information. Reverse diffusion is a learned procedure that turns noise into samples resembling the training data.

    B -->|Add more noise| C[Nearly Gaussian noise]
    C -->|Learned reverse steps| D[Generated image]

The generated image does not have to reproduce a particular training example. In unconditional generation, the model receives neither a real image nor a digit label.

2. Forward diffusion: add noise

The forward process is a Markov chain: the next state depends only on the current state.

The signal is multiplied by a number below one while independent noise is added. Repeating this gradually removes information about the original image.

In our implementation:

# x0: [B, C, H, W]; t: [B], dtype=torch.long

def q_sample(x0, t):
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    alpha_bar = alpha_bars[t].view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
    xt = alpha_bar.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - alpha_bar).sqrt() * eps
    return xt, eps

The reshape broadcasts one noise level across each image. Different images in a batch can have different timesteps. Images, timesteps, and schedule tensors must be on compatible devices.

3. The noise schedule

A schedule specifies how corruption changes over time. The forward schedule is fixed in this project; gradient descent updates the U-Net, not the betas.

Our original setup is:

betas = torch.linspace(0.0001, 0.02, steps=1000)
alphas = 1 - betas
alpha_bars = torch.cumprod(alphas, dim=0)
  • betas increases: each transition adds more noise.
  • alphas decreases slightly: each transition retains slightly less signal.
  • alpha_bars falls toward zero: repeated attenuation removes almost all original signal.

The coefficients multiplying the image and noise are square roots of these variance-related quantities. They are not interchangeable with the quantities themselves.

A useful measure is the signal-to-noise ratio:

4. What the U-Net learns

The network receives a noisy image and its timestep:

(xt,t)⟼ϵθ(xt,t). (x_t,t)\longmapsto\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t). (xt​,t)⟼ϵθ​(xt​,t).

Its output has the same shape as the image. It predicts the noise realization, not a digit class or a single scalar noise level.

Timestep conditioning

The same image pattern can require different treatment at different noise levels. A timestep embedding tells the model which denoising problem it is solving.

Our code maps the timestep into sine and cosine features at multiple frequencies. Each residual block projects that embedding to its channel width and adds it to its image features.

Each residual block uses two 3×3 convolutions, GroupNorm, and SiLU, with timestep conditioning between the convolution stages. An identity or 1×1 projection provides the residual shortcut.

The model has 4,206,593 parameters. Skip connections preserve spatial detail; downsampling lets later features combine information over larger parts of the image.

PyTorch's default MSE averages over batch and image coordinates. This differs from a summed squared norm by a constant factor when image size is fixed.

Training does not run the full reverse chain per example. It uses one sampled noise level and one model prediction. Reducing diffusion steps therefore does not make each training epoch 10× or 100× faster. Generation does use one model evaluation per reverse step.

What we observed

  • Increasing width alone did not clearly improve generation. The wider model at learning rate 0.001 had a large temporary loss spike.
  • Adding the 7×7 level and a second convolution per residual block produced visibly more coherent digits in the 64-sample grids.
  • The 100-step model generated many recognizable digits with 100 model evaluations.
  • The 10-step model also generated recognizable digits, but its grids showed more background noise and rough or malformed strokes.
  • Extending the 10-step run from 25 to 35 epochs reduced training loss slightly; visual quality remained broadly similar.

The architecture change altered several things at once, so it does not isolate which change caused the improvement. The shorter schedules also change the distribution of training noise levels: their lower MSE is not evidence that they are better generators.

What we have not established

We did not track held-out loss during these runs, so we cannot rule out overfitting. A single reconstructed test image is a diagnostic, not a generalization study. Visual inspection of 64 samples is more informative than two samples, but is still qualitative.

For a stronger comparison, evaluate checkpoints on the same held-out images with fixed timestep/noise draws, report loss by noise level, and inspect multiple generated batches. The same seed only reproduces the same random draws within a compatible execution setup; CPU and CUDA generators can differ.

10. Practical reminders

  • Training target: predict the sampled noise, using a timestep for each image.
  • Generation: start from Gaussian noise and traverse every trained reverse step.
  • Final reverse step: do not add fresh noise.
  • Inference: use model.eval() and torch.no_grad().
  • Checkpoint compatibility: architecture and saved schedule must match the trained weights.
  • Display: map [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] to [0,1][0,1][0,1] and clamp only a display copy.
  • Evaluation: training loss, held-out loss, likelihood, and visual quality answer different questions.

From noise to data

title: Markov decision processes
html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

A Markov decision process (MDP) models an agent repeatedly making decisions in an environment.

Agent–environment interaction

st→at→(rt,st+1) s_t\rightarrow a_t\rightarrow(r_t,s_{t+1}) st​→at​→(rt​,st+1​)

At each timestep ttt:

  1. The agent is in state sts_tst​.
  2. It chooses an action ata_tat​.
  3. The environment returns a reward rtr_trt​ and transitions to state st+1s_{t+1}st+1​.
  4. The process repeats.

Formal definition

M=(S,A,P,R,γ) \mathcal M=(\mathcal S,\mathcal A,P,R,\gamma) M=(S,A,P,R,γ)

Component Meaning
S\mathcal SS Set of possible states
A\mathcal AA Set of possible actions
P(s′∣s,a)P(s'\mid s,a)P(s′∣s,a) Probability of reaching state s′s's′ after taking action aaa in state sss
RRR Reward function
γ\gammaγ Discount factor

Markov property

Given the current state and action, predicting the next state does not require the earlier history. The current state contains the information needed for that prediction.

Partial observability

An MDP assumes the agent observes the complete environment state sts_tst​. In robotics, the agent often receives an observation oto_tot​, such as an RGB image, instead.

Quantity Example
State sts_tst​ True robot pose, object pose, velocities, and contact forces
Observation oto_tot​ Camera image

A single image may not reveal the full state: objects can be occluded, velocity may not be visible from one frame, and contact forces may be hidden.

This is a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP).

  • MDP: The agent observes the state sts_tst​.
  • POMDP: The agent observes oto_tot​, generated from the hidden state sts_tst​.

Vision-based robot policies generally operate under partial observability.

title: Generalized advantage estimation
html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

Why advantage estimates matter

Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

PPO is an on-policy actor–critic algorithm designed to improve a policy while discouraging overly aggressive updates. These notes focus on PPO-Clip, the version that uses a clipped surrogate objective.

model.py adapts the PPO script from my pendulum-V1 repo. It trains a continuous-action Gaussian actor and value critic on Pendulum-v1, using GAE and PPO clipping. It reports the environment's raw reward; it does not use the source script's reward shaping. The repository does not include a trained checkpoint or benchmark result.

uv run --extra rl python 03-reinforcement-learning/05-ppo/model.py --episodes 1000

Evaluation runs without a window by default; pass --render to watch it. The tanh action transform's constant scale factor is omitted from the stored log-probability because it cancels in the PPO probability ratio.

PPO at a glance

flowchart TD
    A[Collect fresh rollouts] --> B[Estimate advantages with the critic and GAE]
    B --> C[Update the actor with PPO clipping]
    B --> D[Fit the critic to return targets]
    C --> E[Collect the next batch with the updated policy]
    D --> E
    E --> B
Component Role
Actor πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s) Chooses actions and learns to favor those with positive advantage
Critic Vϕ(s)V_\phi(s)Vϕ​(s) Estimates expected returns and helps compute advantages
GAE A^t\hat A_tA^t​ Estimates how much better or worse an action was than expected
PPO clipping Removes the incentive for excessively large changes in the favored direction

PPO commonly uses Generalized Advantage Estimation to compute advantages. It then performs several epochs of minibatch updates on the collected data, updating both the actor and critic. The old action probabilities remain fixed throughout those updates.

On-policy means each training round uses fresh experience from its rollout policy. Reusing that batch for several optimization epochs is part of PPO; afterward, the updated policy collects a new batch.

The probability ratio

Trajectories are collected using the old policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}πθold​​. During optimization, the current policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ changes while the old policy remains fixed for that batch.

For a sampled state–action pair (st,at)(s_t,a_t)(st​,at​), define:

rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st) r_t(\theta) =\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)} rt​(θ)=πθold​​(at​∣st​)πθ​(at​∣st​)​

The ratio asks: How much more or less likely is the current policy to take the same action in the same state? Here, rtr_trt​ denotes the ratio, not the environment reward. For continuous actions, the ratio uses probability densities.

For example:

πold(at∣st)=0.20,πθ(at∣st)=0.24 \pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a_t\mid s_t)=0.20, \qquad \pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)=0.24 πold​(at​∣st​)=0.20,πθ​(at​∣st​)=0.24

rt=0.240.20=1.2 r_t=\frac{0.24}{0.20}=1.2 rt​=0.200.24​=1.2

The action is now 20% more likely.

Ratio Interpretation
rt=1r_t=1rt​=1 The action’s probability has not changed
rt>1r_t>1rt​>1 The action has become more likely
rt<1r_t<1rt​<1 The action has become less likely

At the start of optimization on a newly collected batch, θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}θ=θold​, so rt=1r_t=1rt​=1.

Combine the ratio with advantage

The advantage estimate A^t\hat A_tA^t​, often computed using Generalized Advantage Estimation, measures whether the sampled action was better or worse than expected under the rollout policy.

  • A^t>0\hat A_t>0A^t​>0: Encourage increasing the action’s probability.
  • A^t<0\hat A_t<0A^t​<0: Encourage decreasing the action’s probability.

The unclipped surrogate objective is:

LCPI(θ)=E^t[rt(θ)A^t] L^{\mathrm{CPI}}(\theta) =\hat{\mathbb E}_t\left[r_t(\theta)\hat A_t\right] LCPI(θ)=E^t​[rt​(θ)A^t​]

Here, E^t\hat{\mathbb E}_tE^t​ means the empirical average over the batch. We maximize this objective, keeping the advantage estimates fixed during the actor update. CPI refers to conservative policy iteration.

Advantage Ratio change Objective contribution Effect
A^t=+5\hat A_t=+5A^t​=+5 1→21\rightarrow21→2 5→105\rightarrow105→10 Increasing a good action’s probability improves the objective
A^t=−5\hat A_t=-5A^t​=−5 1→0.51\rightarrow0.51→0.5 −5→−2.5-5\rightarrow-2.5−5→−2.5 Decreasing a bad action’s probability also improves the objective

Why unrestricted updates are a problem

The unclipped objective keeps rewarding larger changes in the favored direction. For positive advantage, increasing rtr_trt​ keeps increasing rtA^tr_t\hat A_trt​A^t​.

Repeated optimization on the same batch can therefore move the policy far from the policy that collected it. The advantages describe behavior under the old policy, and the surrogate becomes a less reliable guide as the policy and its visited-state distribution change.

PPO modifies the objective to limit the incentive for these large updates.

The clipped surrogate objective

Choose a clipping parameter ϵ\epsilonϵ, for example ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2ϵ=0.2. The clipping interval is then [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2].

LCLIP(θ)=E^t[min⁡(rt(θ)A^t,clip⁡(rt(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t)] L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta) =\hat{\mathbb E}_t \left[ \min\left( r_t(\theta)\hat A_t, \operatorname{clip}\bigl(r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\bigr)\hat A_t \right) \right] LCLIP(θ)=E^t​[min(rt​(θ)A^t​,clip(rt​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t​)]

For each sample, PPO takes the smaller of the unclipped and clipped contributions. The sign of the advantage determines which side becomes flat.

Positive advantage: stop rewarding large increases

Let A^t=+5\hat A_t=+5A^t​=+5 and ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2ϵ=0.2.

rtr_trt​ Unclipped contribution Clipped contribution PPO takes the minimum
1.01.01.0 555 555 555
1.11.11.1 5.55.55.5 5.55.55.5 5.55.55.5
1.21.21.2 666 666 666
2.02.02.0 101010 666 666

Once rt>1+ϵr_t>1+\epsilonrt​>1+ϵ, increasing the probability further gives no additional improvement in this sample’s objective contribution.

Negative advantage: stop rewarding large decreases

Let A^t=−5\hat A_t=-5A^t​=−5 and ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2ϵ=0.2.

rtr_trt​ Unclipped contribution Clipped contribution PPO takes the minimum
1.01.01.0 −5-5−5 −5-5−5 −5-5−5
0.90.90.9 −4.5-4.5−4.5 −4.5-4.5−4.5 −4.5-4.5−4.5
0.80.80.8 −4-4−4 −4-4−4 −4-4−4
0.50.50.5 −2.5-2.5−2.5 −4-4−4 −4-4−4

Because the objective is maximized, −4-4−4 is an improvement over −5-5−5. But once rt<1−ϵr_t<1-\epsilonrt​<1−ϵ, decreasing the probability further gives no additional improvement for this sample.

Why take the minimum instead of just clipping?

Simply clipping the ratio would flatten the objective on both sides, including when the policy moves in the wrong direction. The minimum preserves the penalty for those changes.

For example:

  • Good action made much less likely: With A^t=+5\hat A_t=+5A^t​=+5 and rt=0.5r_t=0.5rt​=0.5, the unclipped contribution is 2.52.52.5 and the clipped contribution is 444. PPO takes 2.52.52.5.
  • Bad action made much more likely: With A^t=−5\hat A_t=-5A^t​=−5 and rt=2r_t=2rt​=2, the unclipped contribution is −10-10−10 and the clipped contribution is −6-6−6. PPO takes −10-10−10.

The per-sample objective can equivalently be written as:

ℓtCLIP={A^tmin⁡(rt,1+ϵ),A^t≥0,A^tmax⁡(rt,1−ϵ),A^t<0. \ell_t^{\mathrm{CLIP}} =\begin{cases} \hat A_t\min\bigl(r_t,1+\epsilon\bigr), & \hat A_t\geq0, \\ \hat A_t\max\bigl(r_t,1-\epsilon\bigr), & \hat A_t<0. \end{cases} ℓtCLIP​={A^t​min(rt​,1+ϵ),A^t​max(rt​,1−ϵ),​A^t​≥0,A^t​<0.​

This is a pessimistic surrogate: it is a lower bound on the unclipped surrogate, not a guarantee about the policy’s actual return. Clipping removes incentives for large beneficial-looking changes while allowing harmful changes to worsen the objective. See Section 3 of the PPO paper.

Clipping is not a hard constraint

PPO does not force every ratio to stay inside [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon][1−ϵ,1+ϵ]. Clipping changes the objective; it does not clamp the policy’s actual probabilities.

A sample’s contribution can become flat while updates from other samples still change its probability through shared parameters.

When using an optimizer that minimizes a loss, the actor loss is typically the negative of this maximization objective:

Lactor=−LCLIP \mathcal L_{\mathrm{actor}}=-L^{\mathrm{CLIP}} Lactor​=−LCLIP

Why use PPO?

PPO combines policy-gradient learning, an actor–critic setup, and a surrogate objective that discourages large policy changes. GAE commonly supplies the advantage estimates.

Compared with TRPO’s explicit constrained optimization, PPO-Clip uses a simpler objective that can be optimized with ordinary first-order gradient methods. This makes it practical for training neural-network policies, although clipping does not guarantee stable learning or monotonic improvement.

title: Soft Actor-Critic
html:
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is an off-policy actor–critic algorithm that combines reward maximization with an entropy bonus. These notes focus on the common continuous-control version with a stochastic actor and two Q-function critics.

SAC at a glance

flowchart TD
    A[Interact with the environment] --> B[Store transitions in a replay buffer]
    B --> C[Sample a minibatch and update both critics]
    C --> D[Update the actor using Q-values and entropy]
    D --> E[Update target critics and optionally temperature]
    E --> A
    E --> C

The replay buffer lets SAC reuse experience collected by earlier policies. The entropy bonus encourages the actor to remain stochastic while seeking high rewards.

Component Role
Actor πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s) Samples actions and learns to balance value with entropy
Critics Qϕ1(s,a)Q_{\phi_1}(s,a)Qϕ1​​(s,a), Qϕ2(s,a)Q_{\phi_2}(s,a)Qϕ2​​(s,a) Estimate the entropy-regularized value of state–action pairs
Replay buffer D\mathcal DD Stores transitions for repeated training
Temperature α\alphaα Controls the weight of entropy relative to reward

Maximum-entropy objective

In the discounted setting, ordinary reward maximization uses:

Jreward(π)=Eτ∼π[∑t=0∞γtrt] J_{\mathrm{reward}}(\pi) =\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi} \left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r_t\right] Jreward​(π)=Eτ∼π​[t=0∑∞​γtrt​]

SAC adds a policy-entropy bonus:

JSAC(π)=Eτ∼π[∑t=0∞γt(rt+αH(π(⋅∣st)))] J_{\mathrm{SAC}}(\pi) =\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t \left(r_t+\alpha\mathcal H\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid s_t)\bigr)\right) \right] JSAC​(π)=Eτ∼π​[t=0∑∞​γt(rt​+αH(π(⋅∣st​)))]

Here, τ\tauτ is a trajectory, γ\gammaγ discounts future rewards and entropy bonuses, and α>0\alpha>0α>0 sets their relative importance.

The goal is to achieve high reward while retaining policy entropy, which can help exploration and discourage premature convergence to a narrow behavior.

Entropy is average surprise

Entropy is the expected negative log-probability of an action sampled from the policy:

H(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)[−log⁡π(a∣s)] \mathcal H\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid s)\bigr) =\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)} \left[-\log\pi(a\mid s)\right] H(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)​[−logπ(a∣s)]

A single −log⁡π(a∣s)-\log\pi(a\mid s)−logπ(a∣s) is a sample of this quantity, not the entropy of the whole distribution.

For a discrete-action example, using natural logarithms:

Action probability Surprise −log⁡π(a∣s)-\log\pi(a\mid s)−logπ(a∣s) Interpretation
0.90.90.9 ≈0.105\approx0.105≈0.105 Expected outcome; little surprise
0.010.010.01 ≈4.605\approx4.605≈4.605 Rare outcome; much more surprise

Entropy averages surprise over all actions, weighted by their probabilities. A rare action’s large surprise does not by itself imply high entropy. A deterministic discrete policy has zero entropy; a more evenly spread discrete policy has higher entropy.

Continuous-action distinction

For continuous actions, π(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s)π(a∣s) is a probability density, and the expression defines differential entropy. Densities may exceed one, so differential entropy can be negative. The discrete rule “deterministic means zero entropy” does not carry over directly; a deterministic continuous policy is a point mass without an ordinary density.

The expectation formula explains SAC’s sampled entropy term:

αH(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)[−αlog⁡π(a∣s)] \alpha\mathcal H\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid s)\bigr) =\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s)} \left[-\alpha\log\pi(a\mid s)\right] αH(π(⋅∣s))=Ea∼π(⋅∣s)​[−αlogπ(a∣s)]

The stochastic actor

The actor samples actions from πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s). A common continuous-control parameterization is a Gaussian followed by a tanh⁡\tanhtanh transformation to bound the actions.

The actor favors actions with high predicted Q-values while also encouraging entropy. Using the two critics, its maximization objective is:

Jπ(θ)=Es∼D, a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[min⁡i∈{1,2}Qϕi(s,a)−αlog⁡πθ(a∣s)] J_\pi(\theta) =\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D,\,a\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)} \left[ \min_{i\in\{1,2\}}Q_{\phi_i}(s,a) -\alpha\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s) \right] Jπ​(θ)=Es∼D,a∼πθ​(⋅∣s)​[i∈{1,2}min​Qϕi​​(s,a)−αlogπθ​(a∣s)]

  • The Q term favors valuable actions.
  • The negative log-density term, averaged over sampled actions, encourages entropy.

States come from replay, but actions for the actor objective are sampled from the current policy. An implementation that minimizes losses uses Lπ=−Jπ\mathcal L_\pi=-J_\piLπ​=−Jπ​.

The critics and soft Bellman target

Unlike the state-value critic V(s)V(s)V(s) in our PPO notes, SAC primarily learns action-value functions Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a).

These are soft Q-functions: under the convention used here, they include expected future entropy bonuses as well as rewards. The current action’s entropy term is added separately in the actor objective.

Why two critics?

SAC learns two separately parameterized critics and uses their minimum:

Qmin⁡(s,a)=min⁡(Qϕ1(s,a),Qϕ2(s,a)) Q_{\min}(s,a) =\min\left(Q_{\phi_1}(s,a),Q_{\phi_2}(s,a)\right) Qmin​(s,a)=min(Qϕ1​​(s,a),Qϕ2​​(s,a))

This helps reduce the overestimation that can arise when policy optimization exploits errors in learned Q-values. The critics share training data, so their errors need not be statistically independent.

Critic target

For a replay transition (s,a,r,s′,d)(s,a,r,s',d)(s,a,r,s′,d), sample a new next-state action:

a′∼πθ(⋅∣s′) a'\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s') a′∼πθ​(⋅∣s′)

Then form the target:

y=r+γ(1−d)[min⁡i∈{1,2}Qϕˉi(s′,a′)−αlog⁡πθ(a′∣s′)] y =r+\gamma(1-d) \left[ \min_{i\in\{1,2\}}Q_{\bar\phi_i}(s',a') -\alpha\log\pi_\theta(a'\mid s') \right] y=r+γ(1−d)[i∈{1,2}min​Qϕˉ​i​​(s′,a′)−αlogπθ​(a′∣s′)]

Here, QϕˉiQ_{\bar\phi_i}Qϕˉ​i​​ are slowly updated target critics. The indicator d=1d=1d=1 means a true terminal state, where future value is zero; a rollout cutoff alone need not be terminal.

Each critic minimizes squared prediction error against the same target:

LQi=E[(Qϕi(s,a)−y)2],i∈{1,2} \mathcal L_{Q_i} =\mathbb E\left[ \left(Q_{\phi_i}(s,a)-y\right)^2 \right], \qquad i\in\{1,2\} LQi​​=E[(Qϕi​​(s,a)−y)2],i∈{1,2}

The expectation covers replay transitions and the sampled next action. The target yyy is held fixed during each critic update. These equations follow the Spinning Up SAC formulation.

Off-policy learning and replay

SAC stores transitions in a replay buffer:

D={(st,at,rt,st+1,dt)} \mathcal D=\left\{(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1},d_t)\right\} D={(st​,at​,rt​,st+1​,dt​)}

It can repeatedly train on transitions collected by earlier policies. The recorded action ata_tat​ trains the critic, while newly sampled current-policy actions are used in the actor objective and next-state target.

This reuse often makes SAC more efficient in environment interactions than on-policy methods such as PPO. It is especially useful when robot interactions are expensive. The advantage depends on the task and implementation; fewer interactions do not necessarily mean less computation or shorter wall-clock training.

Temperature: the reward–entropy balance

Temperature Effect, holding reward scale fixed
Larger α\alphaα Gives entropy more weight and favors more stochastic behavior
Smaller α\alphaα Gives entropy less weight and prioritizes the Q-value term

SAC can use a fixed temperature or learn it automatically to track a target entropy. Automatic tuning increases entropy pressure when entropy is below target and reduces it when entropy is above target. See Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications.

PPO versus SAC

Aspect PPO-Clip SAC
Data use On-policy batches, reused for a few optimization epochs Off-policy transitions reused through replay
Main critic Usually V(s)V(s)V(s) Two soft Q-functions Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a)
Actor signal Advantages, commonly estimated with GAE Q-values plus an entropy term
Main actor objective Clipped probability-ratio surrogate Maximum-entropy objective
Replay buffer Typically no persistent replay across policy iterations Central to training
Environment sample efficiency Often needs more fresh interactions Often benefits from reusing past interactions
Implementation Clipping, advantage estimation, actor and value updates Replay, twin critics, target critics, stochastic actor, optional temperature tuning
Action spaces Commonly used for discrete and continuous actions These notes cover continuous control; discrete variants also exist

PPO emphasizes limiting incentives for large policy updates on fresh rollout data. SAC emphasizes reusing experience to learn Q-values and a reward-seeking, entropy-regularized policy.

Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

act.py implements the action-chunking model described below. train.py includes a synthetic-data pipeline check:

uv run python 04-robot-policies/01-act/train.py --synthetic --epochs 1

The synthetic run checks the code path; it is not a robot success result.

Core Ideas

Small errors in predicted actions can compound into large errors over time.

  • Action chunks: Predict target joint positions for the next kkk timesteps, reducing the effective task horizon by a factor of kkk.
  • Temporal ensembling: Query the policy more frequently and average overlapping action chunks.
  • CVAE training: Train the policy with a reconstruction loss and a term that regularizes the latent distribution toward a Gaussian prior just like VAEs.

CVAE Encoder: Learning the Style Variable

The encoder is a BERT-like transformer. For faster training, it uses proprioceptive observations and action sequences, leaving out images.

Its inputs are:

  1. A learned [CLS] token.
  2. Current joint positions qtq_tqt​.
  3. The demonstrated action sequence AAA of length kkk.

The transformer outputs one vector per input token. The [CLS] output summarizes the sequence and predicts the mean and variance of the style variable zzz.

zzz can capture different ways to perform the same task from the same observation, helping avoid averaging distinct trajectories.

CVAE Decoder: Predicting an Action Chunk

The decoder receives the current observation and zzz and predicts the next kkk actions. It combines ResNet image encoders, a transformer encoder, and a transformer decoder.

1. Encode the observation

  • Images: ResNet18 backbones convert each 480×640×3480\times640\times3480×640×3 RGB image into a 15×20×51215\times20\times51215×20×512 feature map.
  • Flatten: Convert each feature map into a sequence of 300×512300\times512300×512.
  • Spatial information: Add 2D sinusoidal positional embeddings.
  • Joint positions and zzz: Project each to 512 dimensions with linear layers and append them to the image tokens.

The resulting 1202×5121202\times5121202×512 sequence is passed to the transformer encoder.

2. Decode the actions

The transformer decoder takes kkk positional query embeddings of dimension 512. Through cross-attention, these queries attend to the 1202 encoded observation tokens, which supply the keys and values.

The decoder produces a k×512k\times512k×512 sequence. A final MLP maps it to k×14k\times14k×14: target joint positions for the next kkk steps.

Training Loss

  • Reconstruction loss LaL_aLa​: Measures the error between demonstrated and predicted actions.
  • Regularization loss LrL_rLr​: Encourages the encoder's latent distribution to match the Gaussian prior.

Lr=DKL(qϕ(z∣qt,A) ∥ N(0,I)) L_r = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q_\phi(z\mid q_t,A)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I)\right) Lr​=DKL​(qϕ​(z∣qt​,A)∥N(0,I))

Inference

At test time, set zzz to the mean of the prior: zero.

title: Diffusion policy
html:
Implementation Browse the code on GitHub.

model.py implements a transformer-based action denoiser conditioned on PushT observations. train.py trains it and eval.py runs closed-loop rollouts. The example rollout shows one successful episode. See DiT architecture notes for the image-generation model that motivated the backbone.

Related note: ALOHA Unleashed describes another diffusion-based robot policy. It is a paper note, not an implementation in this folder.

Core Ideas

Represent a robot's visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process.

  • Model multimodal action distributions, addressing the concern about distinct action trajectories discussed in ACT.
  • Use action sequences in closed-loop control.
  • Predict actions conditioned on observations without also inferring future states, reducing computation and improving action accuracy.

Adapting DDPM to Robot Actions

DDPMs become diffusion policies through two changes:

  1. The output represents robot actions.
  2. The denoising process is conditioned on robot observations.

CNN Architecture: Temporal U-Net

The example below uses 16 action timesteps, each with 2 action dimensions. Feature shapes are written as timesteps × channels.

1. Project and Condition

  • Project each action into a larger feature dimension.
  • Apply 1D temporal convolutions to mix information between nearby action timesteps.
  • Use FiLM to add conditioning.

Example conditioned features:

h∈R16×256 h\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times256} h∈R16×256

2. Downsample

Downsample along the time dimension. For example:

[16,256]→[8,512] [16,256]\rightarrow[8,512] [16,256]→[8,512]

The next level represents 8 broader temporal regions instead of 16 individual action positions.

3. Upsample with Skip Connections

Upsampling restores a separate feature vector for each action position, now informed by the larger trajectory structure.

Downsampling can lose fine-grained temporal information. Skip connections pass saved features from the downsampling path directly to the corresponding upsampling layers to preserve those details.

The resulting features return to:

hfinal∈R16×256 h_{\mathrm{final}}\in\mathbb{R}^{16\times256} hfinal​∈R16×256

4. Project to Predicted Noise

The final layer maps each 256-dimensional feature vector back to the original 2 action dimensions:

[16,256]→[16,2] [16,256]\rightarrow[16,2] [16,256]→[16,2]

This produces a noise prediction with the same shape as the action sequence.

Limitation: Rapid Action Changes

Temporal convolutions tend to favor low-frequency signals. This likely explains poorer performance when actions change sharply over time, as with velocity commands.

Transformer Architecture

The transformer decoder receives two input sequences:

Input Preparation
Noisy actions AtkA_t^kAtk​ Use actions as tokens and prepend a sinusoidal embedding of diffusion step kkk.
Observation OtO_tOt​ Use a shared MLP to produce an observation embedding sequence that conditions the decoder.

Visual Encoder

Use ResNet-18 without pretraining, with two modifications:

  • Spatial softmax pooling replaces global average pooling to preserve spatial information (Mandlekar et al., 2021).
  • GroupNorm replaces BatchNorm for stable training (Wu & He, 2018).

Noise Schedule and Sampling

Setting Choice
Noise schedule Squared cosine
Sampling method DDIM
Training diffusion steps 100
Inference denoising steps 10

Position vs. Velocity Control

Diffusion Policy performs better with position control than velocity control:

  • Action multimodality is more pronounced in position control.
  • Position control suffers less from compounding errors, making it more suitable for action-sequence prediction.

title: ALOHA Unleashed

Core Architecture

A Transformer-based architecture trained with a diffusion loss, scaling up an encoder–decoder design similar to ACT.

Observation Encoder

1. Encode the Images

  • Resize each of the 4 RGB images to 480×640×3480\times640\times3480×640×3.
  • Feed each image into a separate ResNet50 backbone.
  • Take the stage 4 feature map: 15×20×51215\times20\times51215×20×512 per image.
  • Flatten the spatial dimensions to obtain 1,200 image tokens, each with 512 dimensions, across all four images.

2. Add the Robot State

Project the robot's proprioceptive state—joint positions and gripper values for both arms—into one additional embedding.

This gives 1,201 tokens, each with 512 dimensions.

3. Encode the Tokens

Add positional embeddings and pass the sequence through an 85M-parameter transformer encoder.

The observation latents condition a 55M-parameter transformer decoder with bidirectional attention.

title: VITA Flow Matching
html:
Vision-to-Action Flow Matching (VITA) learns to transform observation latents directly into action latents. Its starting point comes from the observation rather than sampled Gaussian noise.

Motivation

Conventional Diffusion Policy and Flow Matching policies repeatedly inject observations through conditioning modules such as cross-attention, AdaLN, or FiLM.

  • Cross-attention computes interactions between query and observation tokens. Its attention matrix scales with the product of their sequence lengths; this is quadratic when both lengths grow together.
  • AdaLN and FiLM avoid that attention matrix but add feature-modulation operations during generation.

VITA puts observation information into the source latent, removing the need to inject it again through separate conditioning modules at each flow step. “Conditioning-free” describes the flow network’s architecture; the policy still depends on the observation.

The paper reports 1.5–2× faster inference than its conventional conditioned flow-matching baselines, with competitive or better task success rates. This is an experimental comparison, rather than a guaranteed speedup for every implementation.

title: A2A Flow Matching
html:
Action-to-Action Flow Matching (A2A) generates future actions from a starting point informed by the robot’s recent proprioceptive history. The core idea is to use the physical continuity of robot motion to make action generation easier.

Motivation

Starting from random Gaussian noise, as in Diffusion Policy, often requires multiple refinement steps to produce clean actions. This adds inference latency and can become a bottleneck for real-time control.

Two other issues motivate A2A:

  • Proprioceptive information can get diluted. Simply concatenating the current state with high-dimensional image features can overshadow the lower-dimensional proprioceptive signal.
  • Vision alone can be fragile. VITA Flow Matching relies entirely on visual inputs, making it vulnerable to visual distractors in the environment.

From historical actions to future actions

A2A uses historical actions to initialize generation in latent space. Because recent and future robot motions are related, this places the starting distribution closer to the target distribution.

The two input modalities serve different roles:

  • Proprioceptive history provides the starting latent, capturing the robot’s dynamics and temporal continuity.
  • Visual observations condition the flow, providing information about the scene and task.

Keeping these roles separate helps the model use both modalities without letting visual features dominate the proprioceptive signal.
